text.p: Tourists beware -- that innocent souvenir you bought on holiday in some exotic holiday resort could land you in jail when you get back to the European Union.
Stiffer new laws on trade in endangered species come into effect on June 1, officials and environmentalists said on Thursday, bringing with them fines and jail terms.

"In 10 days, we will have a strict and effective law to enhance nature conservation worldwide," Claude Martin, director-general for the World Wide Fund for Nature, told a news conference at Brussels Zaventem airport.
"Now we want to make sure that people comply with it," he said, adding a call to EU countries to commit the resources necessary to implement the new rules.

He was speaking at the launch of an EU-wide publicity campaign intended to warn travellers of the fines and jail sentences they risk for illegally importing into the bloc, often unknowingly, tourist souvenirs bought legally on holiday.

WWF said a quarter of the billions of dollars spent each year in the global wildlife trade went on buying banned items such as rhino horn, big cats' furs, reptile skins, ivory and live animals and plants.

It said the new laws would step up enforcement, cut confusion over implementation within the EU's single market, introduce monitoring requirements for trade in non-threatened species and improve carriage conditions for animals and birds.

Belgian Agriculture Minister Karel Pinxten told the same news conference the legal changes would require extra resources and improved cooperation between government departments and governments themselves. He suggested introducing charges for trade permits as a source of funds.
